## What the reporters noticed

_Eight reporters, each on their own beat. They read the articles above and tell you what they see — suggestion with citations, never proof of anyone's motive._

### Hermes — Pushes back

Same event, 13 outlets, 13 different front doors. Here is how each one leads it: Politico opens with "Trump is weighing whether to grant Canada a tariff reprieve"; CNBC opens with "As U.S.-Canada trade talks collapse, Carney says retaliatory tariffs will start Sept. 8"; NBC News opens with "Trump’s promised tariffs on Canada threaten higher inflation on both sides of the border."; The New York Times opens with "Trump Tariff Talks Leave Key Canadian Official Hopeful".

I read every version, and they are barely the same story. Politico wants you thinking about "Trump is weighing whether to grant Canada a tariff reprieve". CNBC wants you thinking about "As U.S.-Canada trade talks collapse, Carney says retaliatory tariffs will start Sept. 8". NBC News wants you thinking about "Trump’s promised tariffs on Canada threaten higher inflation on both sides of the border.". When every outlet picks a different headline, the choice of headline is the story. Read one and you will feel informed. Read them all and you will realize each one buried somebody else's lead.

### Hades — Pushes back

The coverage reads like the full picture.

It is not. 2 quoted passage(s) and not one of them names its speaker. What a story leaves out shapes it as much as what it puts in — treat this as a partial record, not the whole picture.

### Demeter — Pushes back

Today's news, gone tomorrow — that is how it is presented.

It will outlast the cycle. "and Canada reached deal to delay 50% U.S." (NPR). "and Canada reached deal to delay 50% U.S." (NPR).
